query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Ni content in equimolar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will reduce the immiscibility gap by promoting the earlier dissolution of Cu-rich regions, thereby narrowing the temperature range between premelting onset and complete melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles synthesized as single-phase solid solutions with typical sizes around 60 nm.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one with the baseline equimolar composition and one with a Ni-enriched composition (approximately 10–15% higher Ni while proportionally reducing Cu to maintain overall balance).
generation.conditions: Conduct controlled heating experiments in a high-temperature vacuum furnace with in-situ neutron imaging, acquiring radiographs in 20 °C steps from 1000 °C to 1500 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Local segregation of the lower-melting Cu at the nanoparticle surfaces and interfaces, whose dissolution is facilitated by the increased Ni content.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced Ni acts as a solubility mediator that promotes the dissolution of Cu-rich regions, thereby reducing the persistent immiscibility seen in the liquid state. This leads to a more homogeneous melting process with a smaller temperature gap between premelting and full melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Ni-enriched nanoparticles will display an earlier onset of complete homogeneity (complete melting observed at temperatures ~20–50 °C lower) than the equimolar baseline, with a narrowed temperature range between initial premelting (around 1100 °C) and full melting (around 1420 °C).
generation.baseline: Equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles showing premelting onset around 1100 °C and complete melting near 1420 °C.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for nanoparticles with sizes on the order of tens of nanometers and in systems where no additional segregating phases form due to chemical incompatibility.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the temperature shift may vary due to competing effects from other alloying elements, and the optimal Ni excess required remains to be exactly determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare both equiatomic and Ni-enriched nanoparticles and perform in-situ neutron imaging during controlled heating. Compare radiographs for the onset of Cu-rich premelting and the temperature for complete dissolution.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-enriched nanoparticles do not show a statistically significant (~20 °C or more) lower temperature for complete melting relative to the baseline, or if no difference is observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

The field of high-entropy alloys continues to grow every year, and with this growth comes an enormous amount of never before seen alloy systems with unknown liquid state behavior. As previously shown, neutron imaging can be a very useful technique to elucidate the liquid state behavior of molten alloy systems. With the application of this technique to high-entropy alloys, in-situ imaging of liquid state miscibility has been observed for the first time with the equiatomic additions of Ni to the immiscible CoCrCu system. The current results show the following: Neutron imaging can be utilized to image liquid state behavior in high-entropy alloys. Imaging was carried out on equiatomic CoCrCu buttons with equiatomic additions of Ni such that when melting occurred between the alloying elements, full miscibility was achieved. In-situ neutron imaging was successfully utilized to image in-situ alloying of Ni into an immiscible CoCrCu system. papers.title: In-Situ Imaging of Molten High-Entropy Alloys Using Cold Neutrons.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrCu alloy with equiatomic Ni additions (forming CoCrCuNi) as a high-entropy alloy system.
papers.approach: In‐situ neutron imaging during heating and cooling in a high‐temperature vacuum furnace, capturing radiographs in 20 °C steps.
papers.findings: Observed the onset of melting at ~1100 °C, complete dissolution (alloying and mixing) at ~1420 °C, and solidification at ~1320 °C. The imaging revealed that in the base CoCrCu system, liquid state immiscibility leads to phase-separated liquids (Cu‐rich and CoCr‐rich), and that the addition of Ni enables remixing into a homogeneous liquid phase.
papers.mechanism: Ni acts as a solubility mediator that opens a pathway for Cu to dissolve into the other constituents, thereby converting a phase‐separated liquid into a single-phase alloy. This suggests that the premelting behavior is governed by how alloying additions (here, Ni) modify local atomic interactions, enabling or impeding homogenization during the melting process.

papers.title: Atomic Simulations of Grain Structures and Deformation Behaviors in Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with varying average grain sizes (from 3.6 nm to 2.0 nm).
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations to compute volume–temperature curves and to observe melting processes and deformation mechanisms under uniaxial tension.
papers.findings: Simulations showed that a perfect FCC structure has a melting point around 1940 K, while reducing the grain size leads to a lower melting point (e.g. ~1430 K for 3.6 nm grains and ~1340 K for 2.5 nm grains). At very small grain sizes, significant amorphization occurs, affecting plastic deformation behavior.
papers.mechanism: The melting behavior in nanoparticles is strongly governed by grain size effects. Enhanced grain boundary contributions and defect-induced amorphization lower the effective melting temperature, implying that premelting phenomena may begin at the surfaces and interfaces where atomic coordination differs from the bulk.

papers.title: Mechanical Alloying Behavior and Thermal Stability of CoCrCuFeMnNiₓ High-Entropy Alloy Powders Prepared via MA.
papers.system: CoCrCuFeMnNix high-entropy alloy powders with chemical complexity including Cu and Ni along with other elements.
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying (ball milling) to study diffusion-controlled alloying behavior and phase evolution.
papers.findings: It was observed that during mechanical alloying, elements alloy in a specific sequence (with Cu and Mn alloying first), and that Ni (with its FCC structure and higher plasticity) facilitates the dissolution of other elements. The study underscores that the dissolution and subsequent formation of a homogeneous solid solution depend on the intrinsic melting points and atomic size considerations.
papers.mechanism: The alloying behavior, driven by diffusion rates and atomic size differences, controls chemical homogenization and phase stability. This indicates that during the transition from the premelted state to fully molten and finally resolidified state, kinetic factors (i.e. diffusion and atomic mobility) could be central to governing phase stability.

established: Nanoscale phase transitions in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) display distinct premelting and melting regimes compared to single-metal and bimetallic particles.
In-situ neutron imaging can directly observe the onset of melting, phase separation, and remixing in HEA systems.
Grain size plays a crucial role in determining the melting temperature in nanocrystalline HEAs.
Alloying additions (e.g., Ni) can mitigate liquid immiscibility seen in certain HEA compositions by acting as solubility mediators.

approaches_tried.approach: In-situ neutron imaging during controlled heating/cooling cycles.
approaches_tried.outcome: Captured detailed radiographic evidence of melting onset, phase separation, and remixing, thereby elucidating the interplay between different alloying elements on thermal behavior.

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations of nanocrystalline HEAs with varying grain sizes.
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that a reduction in grain size lowers the melting point and promotes amorphization, highlighting the importance of surface and grain-boundary effects in nanoscale melting dynamics.

approaches_tried.approach: Mechanical alloying experiments to understand diffusion-controlled alloying behavior.
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified a sequence for alloying among elements (e.g., Cu alloys first, followed by Ni facilitating further dissolution), which indirectly informs understanding of solid-solution consolidation upon cooling.

mechanisms: Selective melting initiated by lower-melting-point components (e.g., Cu) starting at surfaces, leading to phase separation that must subsequently be homogenized.
Alloying addition (e.g., Ni) acts as a solubility pathway, promoting remixing of immiscible liquid phases into a homogeneous melt.
Grain-boundary mediated melting, where increased surface-to-volume ratios and defects (especially in smaller grains) lower the melting point and favor amorphization.
Diffusion-controlled alloying kinetics that dictate the sequential dissolution of elements during heating and cooling.
disagreements: The relative influence of surface premelting versus bulk melting in controlling the overall melting behavior remains debated.

While some studies emphasize the role of grain size and boundary effects in lowering melting points, others stress the impact of chemical complexity and diffusion kinetics – the interplay between these factors is not fully resolved.

directions.direction: Composition design – modify the Ni content to test its role as a solubility mediator and its influence on the liquid‐phase remixing of Cu during melting.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the proposed mechanism (Ni‐mediated dissolution of Cu and phase remixing) shown in neutron imaging studies, respects synthesis and particle constraints, and is physically well‐supported by prior work. It is highly feasible with established synthesis and in‐situ imaging methods (e.g., see PMC8320920 records).

directions.direction: Nanoparticle size / microstructure control – vary the nanoparticle (or grain) size to examine surface-to-volume effects and defect density on premelting onset.
directions.assessment: This direction targets the known influence of grain size and surface area on melting point depression (supported by MD studies in PMC6479918). It is feasible by modifying synthesis parameters, and the physics of surface premelting are well understood.

directions.direction: Heat/thermomechanical treatment – control the cooling rate after melting to test if kinetic factors govern the re‐consolidation of the solid solution.
directions.assessment: This approach directly examines if diffusion kinetics and cooling rate affect the final homogeneity. It is informed by diffusion controlled alloying behavior (PMC10144805) and is feasible via controlled furnace protocols.

directions.direction: Defect engineering – alter the defect (twin/grain boundary) density in the nanoparticles to probe how local atomic disorder triggers premelting at surfaces/interiors.
directions.assessment: Targeting the role of defects and surface heterogeneities in initiating premelting, this strategy is physically plausible and is supported by prior simulation and experimental correlations of defect density with melting behavior. It is challenging but experimentally manageable.

directions.direction: Modelling and simulation – develop an atomistic model that couples surface premelting with chemical heterogeneity to predict temperature‐dependent phase homogenization.
directions.assessment: A simulation study could offer predictive insight into the interplay of surface diffusion, chemical segregation, and remixed liquid formation. However, while informative, it is less direct than experiments and may require significant computational validation.
